summary:
Rescue Robots is an interactive, educational survival-and-rescue game set on the Moon and Mars, built as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. Players guide an astronaut through ten lost-robot rescues, five sectors per world, while managing Health, Oxygen, Radiation Risk, Temperature, Energy and Spare Parts. Every decision has a visible cost: repairing a machine spends Energy and a Spare Part, and rerouting power pauses Research. A "Problem → Decision → Cost → Consequence" chain teaches mission-style trade-offs in real time.

The game is grounded in real NASA data. Space weather from NASA DONKI (coronal mass ejections, geomagnetic storms and solar energetic particles) can be replayed as in-game hazards. Curiosity REMS readings from Mars drive the dust-storm scenario, alongside reference figures from NASA fact sheets. Health only drops from oxygen, radiation or temperature, so learners see cause and effect clearly.

It matters because it makes space-environment science tangible and engaging for young learners. It teaches resource management and risk planning without a textbook. It is available in English, Spanish and Portuguese, runs in the browser, and clearly labels game mechanics versus real NASA measurements.
details:
What it does and how it works

Rescue Robots is a survival-and-rescue game for the Moon and Mars. We built it as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. This submission is an interactive web experience that walks through the game's design and lets you play its core mechanics. Each world has five sectors, and each sector hides one lost robot. The goal is to rescue all ten.

The game runs on three connected systems:

  • Survival. Health drops only from three causes: low oxygen, high radiation risk or dangerous temperature. Fixing the cause stops the damage, but repairing a machine does not heal the astronaut. The player has to read the gauges and understand why Health is falling.
  • Repair and resources. The Moon base has several faults and not enough resources to fix them all at once. A repair spends Energy and a Spare Part. Rerouting power from Research to another system pauses Research. A "Problem → Decision → Cost → Consequence" panel shows the trade-off for every choice.
  • Rescue loop. The player locates a robot with the Locator, crosses exposed terrain, repairs the robot and returns to base. The trip costs Health, so planning the way back matters.

Real NASA data

  • NASA DONKI supplies the last 30 days of coronal mass ejections, geomagnetic storms and solar energetic particle events. The player can replay a real event, and the game converts its speed or Kp index into a 0–100 intensity. Above 70, an exposed astronaut loses Health.
  • NASA Curiosity REMS supplies Mars surface temperatures for the dust-storm scenario.
  • NASA fact sheets supply reference values for Moon and Mars temperatures.

Space-weather requests are cached for six hours. If NASA is unreachable, the page falls back to an offline snapshot, so it always works. Every data point is labeled as live, cached or snapshot, and as historical, not real time. Health points and resource percentages are labeled as game mechanics, not NASA measurements.

Benefits and intended impact

Learners see how radiation, temperature, oxygen and solar activity affect astronauts, and they learn it by making decisions, not by reading a list of facts. The game teaches resource management, prioritization and risk planning. It also shows that space weather is real, measured and ongoing. It is free in the browser, with no install or account. It is trilingual (English, Spanish, Portuguese), so it reaches students in more communities.

Tools and technology

  • React 19, TypeScript and Vite 8
  • Three.js with react-three-fiber and drei for the 3D background of Earth, the Moon, Mars, the Sun and dust storms
  • Procedural planet textures generated in a Web Worker, so the page stays res
  • Pixel-art astronaut and robot sprites drawn as SVG from character grids
  • Browser Web Speech API for voiced dialogue lines
  • NASA DONKI and Curiosity REMS data, fetched in the browser
  • Docker, nginx and Dokploy for deployment

We wrote a custom i18n layer and a single stylesheet, with no router, state l

Creativity

The game turns hazards into choices. There is no shield to switch on. Every fix costs something, and the "Problem → Decision → Cost → Consequence" panel makes the consequences visible. A retro pixel-art astronaut and robot sit against a realistic 3D solar system that reacts to the section being viewed and to the data on screen. The "replay a real solar event" slider lets a student pick an actual NASA event and see what it would do to their astronaut.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty. We keep game numbers separate from NASA measurements anive.
  • Language length. Spanish and Portuguese text is 20–30% longer than English. The layout reserves space so it does not jump when the language or state changes. We tested at 390, 1024 and 1440 px.
  • Accessibility. The page supports reduced-motion, keyboard navigation, meter roles on gauges and a fallback when WebGL is unavailable.
  • Performance. There are quality tiers for the 3D scene, with texture generat
  • Reliability. The page shows an offline NASA snapshot when requests fail.
  • Next steps. The Spanish and Portuguese translations were written with AI aneview.
